y-m-31-04.title: What can mean and standard deviation alone tell us for sure?
y-m-31-04.topic: What mean and standard deviation alone can establish
y-m-31-04.goal: Separate certain, possible-but-uncertain, and needing more info when only mean/SD given; find impossible values yourself.
y-m-31-04.material: One grade 9 class 30 students took math test, integer scores 0-100. Mean 70 and standard deviation 5. Individual scores unknown. All 30 are population, so variance (=25) found by dividing by 30. Sum of squared deviations =25×30=750. Figures: 0 100 30 9 70 5 30 25 30 30 25 30 750.
y-m-31-04.thinking.1: Use counterexample show something not necessarily true
y-m-31-04.prereq.0: Mean, deviation, variance, SD meaning (grade 9). Variance is average of squared deviations: sum squares = data count × variance.
y-m-31-04.s.s1.prompt: Choose all claims necessarily true from only mean 70 and SD 5.
y-m-31-04.s.s1.hint.0: For each claim, make 1-2 score lists making it false; check mean and squared-deviation sum.
y-m-31-04.s.s1.hint.1: Assume one score 40; consider how its deviation square fit with total squared deviations.
y-m-31-04.s.s1.r.a: SD 5 no mean every student within 5 points of mean. Some may farther and SD still 5.
y-m-31-04.s.s1.o.b: At least one student score exactly 70.
y-m-31-04.s.s1.r.b: Mean 70 no guarantee someone got 70. Scores 60 and 80 alone can average 70.
y-m-31-04.s.s1.o.c: At least one student score above 70.
y-m-31-04.s.s1.r.c: SD not 0 means not all scores 70. Mean 70: if anyone below, someone else must above. You connect mean and nonzero SD. Figures: 0 70 70 70 0.
y-m-31-04.s.s1.r.d: Mean and median may differ; mean/SD alone no tell middle score.
y-m-31-04.s.s1.r.e: Deviation ≥30 means one squared deviation ≥900, greater than total 750, impossible. Good use fixed sum of squares.
y-m-31-04.s.s1.explain: Sum squared deviations fixed 750, so one student's square no exceed 750. Score 40 deviation -30 square 900, impossible. SD nonzero means scores not all same; mean 70 means someone above 70. Median, whether someone got 70, and all between 65-75 cannot be known alone. Figures: 750 750 40 -30 900 0 70 70 70 65 75.
y-m-31-04.s.s2.prompt: Enter 3 different scores definitely impossible for one student here. (Integer 0-100)
y-m-31-04.s.s2.hint.0: Choose candidate score; calculate squared deviation; check fit within all deviations' squared sum.
y-m-31-04.s.s2.hint.1: For scores 45 and 60, test whether list can still have mean 70 and SD 5.
y-m-31-04.s.s2.ok.c2: If any student had this score, mean 70 and squared-deviation sum 750 cannot both hold.
y-m-31-04.s.s2.fail.c2: This score is possible; make list where this student and others fit mean and squared-sum.
y-m-31-04.s.s2.explain: One student's squared deviation cannot exceed 750; other 29 deviations must cancel it, so practically max around 725. Therefore scores 43 or less and 97 or more impossible. 20,35,100 easy to rule out; 43,97 boundary need careful calculation. But 45 possible: one gets 45, five get 75, 24 get 70; mean 70, SD 5. Figures: 750 29 725 43 97 20 35 100 43 97 45 45 75 70 70 5.
y-m-31-04.s.s3.prompt: Friend says 'SD 5, so every score between 65 and 75.' Use concrete counterexample explain not necessarily true; write extra info needed to check.
y-m-31-04.s.s3.hint.0: Make score list with some outside 65-75, check mean and squared deviations fit.
y-m-31-04.s.s3.hint.1: What score info needed to verify every student is in range?
y-m-31-04.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. Not necessarily true. For example, ...
y-m-31-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: In example, you check mean 70 and SD 5 really fit?
y-m-31-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Use one counterexample enough to break 'every student'?
y-m-31-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: State exact info needed to check claim?
y-m-31-04.s.s3.model.0: Not necessarily. Example one student 45, five 75, other 24 score 70; mean 70, SD 5, but someone has 45. Need individual scores or minimum/maximum.
y-m-31-04.s.s3.model.1: SD only represents typical distance from mean. Some may be outside 65-75, so cannot say everyone inside. Need score distribution/frequency table.
y-m-31-04.s.s3.model.2: Even with outside 65-75, mean 70 and SD 5 possible. Example one 45, five 75, other 24 70. Need each person's score to check.

y-m-31-08.thinking.1: Make several cases wey meet conditions
y-m-31-08.title: If combine class averages, is that the overall average?
y-m-31-08.goal: Learn two group means alone no determine combined mean; say student counts also needed, and make class size examples.
y-m-31-08.material: Class A mean 70, B mean 80 (same test, at least 1 student each). Want combined mean. Soyul says average of 70 and 80, namely 75, must be overall mean. Student counts unknown.
y-m-31-08.thinking.2: State when generalization (mean of means) works
y-m-31-08.prereq.0: Meaning of mean: total divided by number of values (grade 7)
y-m-31-08.s.s1.prompt: Choose fitting explanation of Soyul statement and combined mean.
y-m-31-08.s.s1.hint.0: Put numbers one at a time; compare total score sums if class sizes equal or A much bigger.
y-m-31-08.s.s1.hint.1: What can you find by multiplying each class mean by student count?
y-m-31-08.s.s1.o.a: I think 75, halfway between means, must be combined mean.
y-m-31-08.s.s1.r.a: Different class sizes have different weight. If one class much bigger, combined mean closer to that class mean.
y-m-31-08.s.s1.o.b: Combined mean between 70 and 80, but need student counts for exact value.
y-m-31-08.s.s1.r.b: You note combined mean between means and exact value needs counts.
y-m-31-08.s.s1.o.c: Even without counts, B mean higher so combined mean must exceed 75.
y-m-31-08.s.s1.r.c: Even if B mean higher, many more students in A can make mean below 75. Check counts.
y-m-31-08.s.s1.o.d: Think exact overall mean can be calculated from 70 and 80 alone.
y-m-31-08.s.s1.r.d: Means alone no tell each class total. Multiply mean by student count to get score sum.
y-m-31-08.s.s1.explain: Each sum=(mean)×(count), so overall=(70a+80b)/(a+b). It is 75 only if counts equal. More students in either class pulls mean toward 70 or 80; always between. 70 80
y-m-31-08.s.s2.prompt: Choose counts a,b for A,B (integers 1–40) so combined mean 72–74. Make 3 cases with different ratios; (20,10) and (10,5) same ratio, count once. 10 10 20 5
y-m-31-08.s.s2.hint.0: Which class needs more students to pull mean toward 70?
y-m-31-08.s.s2.hint.1: Choose counts, calculate (70a+80b)/(a+b), check 72–74. Same-ratio pairs count once.
y-m-31-08.s.s2.fail.c2: Combined mean no be 72 to 74. Check (70a+80b)/(a+b).
y-m-31-08.s.s2.explain: If A has 1.5 to 4 times as many students as B, mean is 72–74. (30,10) gives 72.5; (20,10) about 73.3; (6,4) exactly 74. (10,10) gives 75 and (10,30) gives 77.5, outside. 10 10 10 10 10 20 30 30 4 6
y-m-31-08.s.s3.prompt: Say when Soyul claim that mean of means equals overall mean is right or wrong.
y-m-31-08.s.s3.hint.0: For equal and unequal class sizes, write total as mean×count and compare.
y-m-31-08.s.s3.hint.1: Use sample counts like 20 and 10 and calculate combined mean directly.
y-m-31-08.s.s3.placeholder: For example, when class counts ..., it works; when ..., it does not.
y-m-31-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: You state both when right and when wrong?
y-m-31-08.s.s3.selfAssess.2: You explain using total scores divided by total students?
y-m-31-08.s.s3.model.0: If equal counts, 75 is correct. If different, mean moves toward bigger class. Example A 30, B 10: (2100+800)÷40=72.5, not 75.
y-m-31-08.s.s3.model.1: Only if class sizes equal does average of two means equal combined mean. If counts differ, combined mean leans toward class with more students.
y-m-31-08.s.s3.modelNote.1: Answer explains reason in words without numeric example.

y-m-31-01.title: Find where Minseo solution wrong
y-m-31-01.topic: Check solution about variance and standard deviation
y-m-31-01.goal: Find wrong line in variance/SD solution, use clue to spot strange answer without full recalculation, and make new data set with same mean and variance.
y-m-31-01.material: Scores for 5 students in Minseo group: 4,7,5,8,11 points. Minseo solution below finds spread. One line wrong. These 5 are whole population, so variance divide by 5. [4 5 7 8]
y-m-31-01.thinking.0: Find error by checking reason for every solution line
y-m-31-01.thinking.2: Make new data set meeting all conditions
y-m-31-01.prereq.1: Variance and standard deviation: mean squared deviations is variance; positive square root is SD (Grade 9). Data are all students, so divide by count.
y-m-31-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose wrong line in Minseo solution.
y-m-31-01.s.s1.hint.0: Line by line, say how each number came from prior line.
y-m-31-01.s.s1.hint.1: Recalculate each line and compare final number with previous line.
y-m-31-01.s.s1.explain: Line 6 wrong. Lines through 5 calculate correctly. Negative deviations in line 2 normal when scores below mean; sum of deviations always 0 when mean correct. Line 6 copied variance 6 as SD. SD na positive square root of variance, not variance itself, so √6 (around 2.4 points). [3]
y-m-31-01.s.s2.prompt: Before recalculating line 6, choose all clues to doubt am.
y-m-31-01.s.s2.hint.0: Put SD size beside deviations −3,0,−2,1,4 and compare. [0 1 2 3 5]
y-m-31-01.s.s2.hint.1: Write units for variance and SD and check if same.
y-m-31-01.s.s2.o.a: Negative values like −3 and −2 dey in deviations
y-m-31-01.s.s2.r.a: Deviation negative when score below mean. Squared and added, negatives no make solution wrong.
y-m-31-01.s.s2.o.b: Standard deviation 6 bigger than biggest deviation size 4
y-m-31-01.s.s2.r.b: You notice representative deviation size no fit exceed biggest individual deviation. Good check compared result size with data.
y-m-31-01.s.s2.o.c: There are 5 data, dividing by 5 for variance seem wrong
y-m-31-01.s.s2.r.c: All 5 surveyed; division by count 5 is convention here. No issue.
y-m-31-01.s.s2.o.d: Variance and standard deviation both 6, but units points² and points
y-m-31-01.s.s2.r.d: Good check: different-unit quantities same number look strange. Unit change from variance to SD.
y-m-31-01.s.s2.o.e: Feels strange all deviations sum to 0
y-m-31-01.s.s2.r.e: Deviation sum always 0 if mean calculated correctly. Zero show earlier steps right. [0]
y-m-31-01.s.s2.explain: Two clues without redoing everything: SD represents typical deviation size, so cannot exceed largest deviation size (here 4), but result 6. Also variance unit points² and SD unit points differ, yet same number written. Negative deviations, dividing by 5, and sum 0 are all normal.
y-m-31-01.s.s3.prompt: Make 5 scores different from original (4,5,7,8,11) but mean 7 and variance 6. Integer scores 0–15; repeats allowed. Make 2 different data sets. (Order-only difference same data.) [4 5 7 8]
y-m-31-01.s.s3.hint.0: First determine total for 5 scores, then place scores so deviations from mean spread between −3 and 4.
y-m-31-01.s.s3.hint.1: After choosing scores, square deviations and check total 30.
y-m-31-01.s.s3.fail.c2: Mean no be 7. Check sum of 5 scores.
y-m-31-01.s.s3.fail.c3: Variance no be 6. Check squared-deviation total.
y-m-31-01.s.s3.explain: For example, 3,6,7,9,10 sum 35 and squared-deviation sum 16+1+0+4+9=30, so variance 6. 4,4,9,9,9 and 5,5,5,10,10 also work. Same mean/variance no mean data same. [10 3 4 4 5 5 5 6 7 9 9 9]

y-m-31-02.title: Ice cream and swimming accidents: how far can we say?
y-m-31-02.goal: Read how two variables move together, revise causal judgment as information comes, and separate what correlation alone can and cannot show.
y-m-31-02.material: In Seaside Town, monthly ice cream sales (thousands) and beach swimming accidents recorded March–August. Monthly (sales, accidents): March (9,2), April (14,3), May (20,5), June (26,7), July (34,10), August (36,11). Imagine scatter plot sales horizontal, accidents vertical. [10 11 14 2 20 26 3 34 36 5 7 9]
y-m-31-02.thinking.1: Revise judgment/confidence when new data show
y-m-31-02.prereq.0: Identify positive, negative, no correlation in scatter plot (Grade 8–9)
y-m-31-02.s.s1.prompt: Data added one piece at a time. Each time choose your thought.
y-m-31-02.s.s1.hint.0: At each step choose 2–3 table numbers and compare how other value move when one rise.
y-m-31-02.s.s1.hint.1: Separate whether new info change “move together” fact or explanation for it.
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.0.ask: What shape the 6 scatter points make?
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.0.after: As sales rise, accidents tend to rise, points go upper right. They cluster close, so correlation strong.
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.0.o.a: Points go lower right; months with higher sales tend to have fewer accidents
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Check table: as sales rise, accidents increase or decrease?
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.0.o.b: All points lie exactly on one line
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.0.r.b: Sales rise 5 from 9 to 14, accidents rise 1; sales rise 6 from 14 to 20, accidents rise 2, so increase not constant. Points gather around line, not exactly on it.
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.0.o.c: Points go upper right; months with higher sales tend to have more accidents
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You read sales and accidents tend to rise together: positive correlation.
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.0.o.d: Points scattered with no clear direction
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.0.r.d: Compare March and August. No direction wrong; sales and accidents move together.
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.1.info: City official say, “Ice cream sales and accidents rise together, so reduce ice cream sales and swimming accidents go down.”
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.1.ask: Wetin you think about this claim?
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.1.after: Seeing correlation no prove one cause the other. Hidden factor may affect both; to confirm cause, need another method.
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Hard to call cause just because they rise together. Another factor may affect both
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You separate correlation and causation, and consider hidden factor.
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Correlation clear, so say reducing sales will reduce accidents
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Moving together and causing each other are different. Table no say accidents really decrease if sales cut.
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Table alone can't tell, so reduce sales and see if accidents change
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You avoid causal claim from observed data alone and propose test. Think too conditions must be controlled carefully.
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Hard to believe correlation at all; table numbers maybe chance
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.1.r.d: Six points clearly show tendency to rise together. Correlation and causal explanation different. [6]
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.2.info: You look up average monthly temperature too: March 6°C, April 12, May 18, June 23, July 27, August 28. Temperature and accidents, and temperature and sales, both rise together.
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.2.ask: Add this info and sort out your thought.
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.2.after: Temperature move with both sales and accidents, so it may explain their rise together. Still, to say sales have no effect at all on accidents need more data/experiment.
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.2.o.a: This table prove temperature cause accidents for sure, no more investigation
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Temperature also only shows correlation. Other factors like visitor numbers may matter; too early to call proof.
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Once temperature known, sales-accident correlation disappear, so unrelated
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Even with temperature, scatter shape between sales and accidents same. Correlation remains; interpretation changes.
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.2.o.c: With temperature added, official first claim reducing sales reduces accidents still believable
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.2.r.c: A factor like temperature that affects both now appears. First claim has weaker basis.
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Temperature may affect both, but too early to say sales unrelated to accidents
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You account for new data and adjust confidence.
y-m-31-02.s.s1.reflect: In step 2, how my thought change with step 3 data? If it stayed same, say how new data changed confidence.
y-m-31-02.s.s2.prompt: Reply to official in 2–3 sentences. Cite at least one table number and judge proposal “reduce sales, accidents go down”.
y-m-31-02.s.s2.hint.0: Choose month with fewest sales and most sales, write accidents and temperatures side by side.
y-m-31-02.s.s2.hint.1: First state what must be confirmed for proposal to be right.
y-m-31-02.s.s2.placeholder: e.g. Contrary to your proposal, table shows ...
y-m-31-02.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Are numbers/evidence I gave actually from table?
y-m-31-02.s.s2.selfAssess.2: You suggest what official should check next?
y-m-31-02.s.s2.model.0: March: sales 9, accidents 2; August: 36 and 11, so both rise. But warmer months may raise both, so hard to claim reducing sales would reduce accidents.
y-m-31-02.s.s2.model.1: Table show hotter months have higher sales and accidents (August 28 degrees, 11 accidents). No evidence ice cream causes accidents yet; check other factors like visitor numbers.
y-m-31-02.s.s2.modelNote.1: This answer uses temperature evidence and proposes more checking.
y-m-31-02.s.s2.model.2: August sales 36 thousand, accidents 11, so both rise, but can't say reducing sales cuts accidents. Another factor like temperature may affect both.

y-m-31-03.title: The mean went up but the middle stayed same
y-m-31-03.topic: Different changes in mean and median
y-m-31-03.goal: Make case yourself where only some scores change so mean change but median stay same; explain how the two values tell different things.
y-m-31-03.material: 5 students performance scores: 60,65,70,75,80. Mean and median both 70. Grading rules change; only 60-point and 80-point students get re-marked. Call new scores a,b (integers 0-100); other 65,70,75 stay. After re-marking, mean rise at least 4 from 70, median still 70. Figures: 5 60 65 70 75 80 70 60 80 0 100 65 70 75 4 70 70.
y-m-31-03.thinking.0: Separate what conditions require and what not
y-m-31-03.thinking.1: Make several cases meeting all conditions
y-m-31-03.thinking.2: Choose representative value fitting situation and explain why
y-m-31-03.prereq.1: For 5 values sorted by size, middle one na median
y-m-31-03.s.s1.prompt: Choose every statement we must accept in situation above.
y-m-31-03.s.s1.hint.0: For each statement, make new (a,b) pair making am false; identify one you cannot make false that way.
y-m-31-03.s.s1.hint.1: Make table: sort 65,70,75,a,b and see where a,b must dey compared with 70 for 70 to stay middle. Figures: 65 70 75 70 70.
y-m-31-03.s.s1.o.a: New scores a+b total at least 160.

y-m-31-03.s.s1.r.c: Case (60→60,80→100) still get 3 students 70+, so no guarantee count increase. Figures: 60 60 80 100 70 3.
y-m-31-03.s.s1.o.d: At least one new score 90 or above.
y-m-31-03.s.s1.r.d: Sum at least 160, but one score must be 70 or below; good reasoning about how big other score must be.
y-m-31-03.s.s1.o.e: Both former 60 and 80 students get higher new scores.
y-m-31-03.s.s1.r.e: One changed score may stay same or drop. Check case where former 60 score stays 60.

Conditions work if one score stay same, like (60,100), so last statement (both scores rose) not necessarily true. Figures: 4 20 160 70 70 70 70 90 160 60 100 60 80.

y-m-31-03.s.s3.hint.1: For mean and median each, write one line 'what this value alone tells' and compare.

y-m-31-05.title: If both SDs equal 6, are spreads equal?
y-m-31-05.topic: Compare spread when data use different units
y-m-31-05.goal: Judge whether SD numbers for two unit-different data sets can be directly compared; explain method and conditions needed.
y-m-31-05.material: School nurse measure height and weight of 20 classmates. Height mean 160 cm, SD 6 cm; weight mean 52 kg, SD 6 kg. Jihu says, 'Both SDs 6, so height and weight spread same degree!'
y-m-31-05.thinking.0: Judge while considering what numbers mean (units)
y-m-31-05.prereq.0: Larger SD means data spread wider around mean (grade 9)
y-m-31-05.prereq.1: Length units m and cm relation (1 m=100 cm)
y-m-31-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose best thought about Jihu claim.
y-m-31-05.s.s1.hint.0: For height and weight, write unit for each SD 6.
y-m-31-05.s.s1.hint.1: Write height in m; calculate new mean and SD.
y-m-31-05.s.s1.o.a: Both SD numbers 6, so data spread equally.
y-m-31-05.s.s1.r.a: SD number change with units; can't directly compare 6 cm and 6 kg as same value.
y-m-31-05.s.s1.o.b: Height has larger mean and spreads by 6, so more spread than weight
y-m-31-05.s.s1.r.b: Larger mean no mean larger spread. Relative to mean, 6 fit look different size.
y-m-31-05.s.s1.o.c: One cm, other kg; hard compare number 6 directly.
y-m-31-05.s.s1.r.c: You note different-unit SDs no compare by number alone.
y-m-31-05.s.s1.o.d: Weight, where 6 is bigger share of mean, relatively more spread.
y-m-31-05.s.s1.r.d: Compare share relative to mean (6÷160 vs 6÷52). Valid if standard chosen, but not comparing SD numbers themselves.
y-m-31-05.s.s1.explain: Hard to directly compare SD values with different units because unit changes number. Choose separate unit-free standard, like share of mean, to compare.
y-m-31-05.s.s1.acc.0: Relative-to-mean method: 6÷160≈3.8%, 6÷52≈11.5%, valid; but that's a different standard, not direct SD comparison.
y-m-31-05.s.s2.prompt: New info: write height in m rather than cm; mean 1.6m, SD 0.06m. Weight stays mean 52kg, SD 6kg. What can you say now?
y-m-31-05.s.s2.hint.0: Write one student's 160 cm height in m; consider if same change applies to everyone.
y-m-31-05.s.s2.hint.1: If weight written in g, what would SD be?
y-m-31-05.s.s2.o.a: SD 0.06 far below 6, so height hardly spreads, weight much more
y-m-31-05.s.s2.r.a: Check whether conclusion should change just by changing units of same height. Looking only at numbers flips conclusion each time units change.
y-m-31-05.s.s2.o.b: Only unit changed; spread same, so don't judge side-by-side SD numbers.

y-m-31-07.title: Result say no correlation. But truly no relation at all?
y-m-31-07.topic: Scatterplot relationships wey no be straight line
y-m-31-07.goal: Understand "no correlation" means no straight-line trend; make nonlinear data to correct friend conclusion.
y-m-31-07.material: 8 students report sleep hours x and focus y (0–10): (4,3),(5,5),(6,8),(7,9),(8,9),(9,8),(10,5),(11,3). Points no lean one way: focus no generally rise/fall with longer sleep. Friend Hayun says no correlation means sleep time no relation with focus. 10 11 3 3 4 5 5 5 6 7 8 8 8 8 9 9 9
y-m-31-07.thinking.0: Check claim scope: straight-line trend versus any relationship
y-m-31-07.prereq.0: Scatterplots and positive, negative, no correlation (middle-school level) 8 9
y-m-31-07.prereq.1: Read pair (sleep, focus) as plotted point
y-m-31-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose best thought about Hayun conclusion.
y-m-31-07.s.s1.hint.0: Read sleep hours 4 to 11 in order and write how focus change.
y-m-31-07.s.s1.hint.1: Find sleep time with highest and lowest focus; compare.
y-m-31-07.s.s1.o.a: Think if points no form straight line, there cannot be any relation.
y-m-31-07.s.s1.r.a: Values can relate in shape other than straight line. Read table in order.
y-m-31-07.s.s1.o.b: No correlation only means no tendency to lean; another shaped relation can exist.
y-m-31-07.s.s1.r.b: You point out no correlation is not same as no relationship.
y-m-31-07.s.s1.o.c: Think 8 points too few to say anything about relation.
y-m-31-07.s.s1.r.c: Even 8 points show clear shape: high at medium sleep, low at both ends. Little data means be careful, not say nothing.
y-m-31-07.s.s1.o.d: Think focus keep rising with sleep time, so say positive correlation.
y-m-31-07.s.s1.r.d: Look: focus low at 10 and 11 hours. It no keep rising with long sleep.
y-m-31-07.s.s1.explain: No correlation means points no lean one way in straight-line pattern. But this data clearly relate: too little/much sleep gives low focus, appropriate sleep high. No straight-line trend does not mean unrelated.
